in-pusiostoma-mendicaria.title: Bumble Bee Snail
in-pusiostoma-mendicaria.sci: Pusiostoma mendicaria (also listed as Engina mendicaria)
in-pusiostoma-mendicaria.summary: A tiny black-and-yellow banded snail that scavenges leftovers and burrows in the sand.
rows: About 1-1/2 in; Wikipedia gives a shell of 10–20 mm (0.4–0.8 in)
Carnivore scavenger. Uneaten meaty food, decaying matter and small sand worms
Red Sea and Indian Ocean across the tropical Indo-Pacific to northern Australia

in-nassarius-sp.title: Nassarius Snail
in-nassarius-sp.summary: A burrowing scavenger snail that pops out of the sand, siphon first, when it smells food.
rows: Carnivore scavenger. Leftover food, detritus and decaying matter
notes: Lives buried in the sand with only its siphon showing; needs a sand bed.
Works well in a small group.

in-astraea-tecta.title: Star Turbo Snail (Astraea Snail)
in-astraea-tecta.summary: A cone-shelled grazing snail that cleans algae off live rock.
rows: About 1 in; wild record 6 cm (2.4 in) DL (SeaLifeBase)
Herbivore. Film and hair algae on rocks and glass

in-conomurex-luhuanus.title: Strawberry Conch
in-conomurex-luhuanus.summary: A sand-sifting conch with an orange lip. Also sold as Orange Lip or Tiger Conch. It moves with a hopping motion.
rows: About 3 in; wild record 8 cm (3.1 in) SHL (SeaLifeBase)
Omnivore. Algae and detritus on the sand bed
notes: Needs a sand bed to forage in.

in-cerithium-snail.title: Cerith Snail
in-cerithium-snail.summary: Small cone-shelled snails that graze algae, diatoms and film off rock and glass and burrow through the sand. A hardy, reef-safe clean-up crew snail.
rows: Herbivore/detritivore: algae, diatoms, film and leftover food
Tropical seas; shallow reefs and lagoons
notes: Stirs the top layer of sand, which helps keep it clean.

in-trochus-snail.title: Trochus Snail
in-trochus-snail.summary: A cone-shaped top (turban) snail that grazes algae on rock and glass. Hardy, reef safe and easy to keep.
rows: Algae grazer: forages algae on live rock and glass
notes: Keep away from crabs and fish that eat snails.

in-nerita-snail-marine.title: Nerite Snail (saltwater)
in-nerita-snail-marine.summary: Small round-shelled snails from rocky shores that graze algae. Hardy and reef safe, but they like to crawl above the waterline.
rows: Tropical rocky shores and intertidal zones
notes: Keep a tight-fitting lid on the tank: it can climb or jump out.

in-strombus-fighting-conch.title: Fighting Conch
in-strombus-fighting-conch.sci: Strombus sp. (S. alatus or S. pugilis)
in-strombus-fighting-conch.summary: A sand-dwelling Atlantic conch that grazes algae and detritus off the sand bed. Peaceful and reef safe; its "fighting" name comes from how it pushes itself along.
rows: Usually 1–2 in sold; shells reach about 4 in (11 cm)
Herbivore/detritivore: algae and detritus on the sand; add sinking algae food if needed
Western Atlantic: Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico and Florida
notes: Needs an open sand bed to graze.

in-lambis-spider-conch.title: Spider Conch
in-lambis-spider-conch.summary: A large Indo-Pacific sea snail with six long, finger-like spines on its shell. It sifts sand and grazes film algae, detritus and some cyanobacteria.
rows: Usually about 7–9 in; up to about 12 in including spines
125 gal or larger, established, with a deep sand bed
Yes, but it can knock over loose rocks and frags
Grazer: film algae, red and hair algae, detritus and cyanobacteria; add sinking algae pellets or spirulina if needed
Indo-Pacific, from East Africa to French Polynesia and Japan
notes: Moves by "hopping" with its strong foot and may vanish under the sand for long periods.
